🔔 Bitcoin price nears Fidelity’s power law support: Accumulation zone or missing catalyst? 

📌 On his power law model, a logarithmic chart that bounds Bitcoin’s entire price history between an upper resistance curve, a middle trendline, and a lower support curve, the floor currently sits near 58,000 dollars. That lower line has caught every major Bitcoin bottom since 2015. Timmer’s label for the zone the market has now entered is unambiguous: accumulation. His caveat is just as unambiguous: he sees no catalyst for a reversal, and he is not calling a bottom.

⚠️ That combination, a historically reliable floor approaching and a strategist refusing to ring the bell, is the most honest summary of the Bitcoin market in July 2026. The asset is coming off its worst quarter since the 2022 bear market, spot ETFs just recorded their largest quarterly outflow since launch, the speculative premium that carried the price past 120,000 dollars last year has evaporated, and the fast money has visibly rotated elsewhere, first into gold, then into semiconductor stocks. And yet the two quantitative measures Timmer trusts most, the deviation from the power law trendline and the Bitcoin-to-gold ratio, have both sunk to depths recorded at exactly two prior moments: the 2018 low and the 2022 low. Both of those moments were generational buying opportunities. Both also felt like the end of the world at the time.

🔖 This feature takes the model seriously in both directions: what the power law actually says, why its track record earns attention, and why the missing-catalyst objection is not a hedge but the core of the analysis.

🖥 Pakistan, Iran pledge joint efforts for regional peace as interior ministers meet in Islamabad

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Pakistan’s Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi says that his country and Islamic Republic of Iran will work together to achieve regional peace and advance the welfare of their two nations, as senior delegations from both countries held formal talks in Islamabad.

The high-level meeting was co-chaired by Iranian Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni and his Pakistani counterpart, Mohsin Naqvi.
​
Naqvi said the presence of senior representatives from Iran’s Ministries of Industry, Mine and Trade, Oil, Agricultural Jihad, and Roads and Urban Development at the meeting reflected the importance of bilateral cooperation and new measures to open fresh avenues for it.
​
“Our view of this important visit is a good news for the region,” Naqvi said, welcoming Momeni’s first official trip to the Pakistani capital.
​
“Iran and Pakistan will work together for the development and welfare of the peoples of both countries, as well as for the establishment of peace in the region,” he said.
​
Naqvi also addressed the threat of terrorism along the shared border.
​
“Tehran and Islamabad are determined to control this challenge and will not allow terrorists and their supporters to succeed in their objectives,” he said, adding that close coordination between the two countries’ security agencies was essential to eradicate anti-security elements, particularly their financial backers.
​
He also raised the issue of human trafficking along the shared border, stressing the need for bilateral cooperation to prevent the use of sea routes for smuggling.
​
On trade, Momeni presented three priority areas: streamlining commercial truck transit between the two countries, raising bilateral trade to $10 billion, and modernizing the railway line on the Pakistani side of the border.
​
“The Iranian side has built the railway to near Mirjaveh,” Momeni said, adding that Iran expected Pakistani authorities to give serious attention to upgrading the line on the Taftan side of the border.
​
He also called on Pakistan to take steps to expand border trade activity at the Rimdan crossing.
​
Iranian delegation members raised additional proposals, including opening banking relations to facilitate trade, expanding exports of Iranian petroleum products to Pakistan, agricultural cooperation, developing corridor links, including the North-South Corridor, and forming a joint committee to resolve trade issues, centered on Sistan-and-Baluchestan province and Pakistan’s Balochistan province.
​
Noting Tehran and Islamabad’s shared will to sign a free trade agreement, the Iranian delegation said that if amendments to the initial text are needed, Iran is ready for close cooperation to advance this stage.
​
The Iranian side also indicated readiness to build cold storage facilities and a slaughterhouse at a Pakistani border point to support livestock and meat trade, while Naqvi suggested the matter could be discussed further between the governors of Sistan-and-Baluchestan and Pakistan’s Balochistan province.
​
Naqvi announced that both sides were committed to operationalizing a sea route between Chabahar and Gwadar.
​
“We are determined to make the maritime route between Chabahar and Gwadar operational and can use this route as another step toward developing bilateral trade,” he said.
​
The Iranian delegation also reported talks with Pakistan’s civil aviation authority, saying Iran is ready to facilitate Pakistan’s aviation needs.
